<reason>Both sides built coherent cases, but B progressively won the decisive clashes. A's core asymmetry (a lab-made pathogen exists certainly in a freezer today vs. speculative benefits) was strong and stayed live, and A's pressure question on deployed vaccines forced a real concession. However, B absorbed that concession cleanly by reframing it as retrospective certainty demanded of prospective science, then landed the debate's most damaging sequence: the BWC distinction (banning a weapon with no defensive use vs. banning defensive work itself), the nature-frequency counter (five flu pandemics, COVID — which A never answered), and above all the "surveillance network" turn showing that A's own enforcement signals (grants, publications, whistleblowers, prestige-chasing researchers) depend on the legal research ecosystem the ban extinguishes. A's reply that visibility "only sees the compliant" repeated the original claim without engaging B's chokepoint argument, and A never articulated the potentially winning counter that ordinary natural-virology work remains legal and preserves those signals. B's answers to pressure questions (A1/A2) were direct and structural; A's answers were adequate but fed B's contradiction framing. B closed by crystallizing the clash; A's closing was punchy but largely recapitulative.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.4–B4.5: B observed that PRO's enforcement model runs on human signals — grants, publications, whistleblowers — every one of which exists only when research is legal and above ground, concluding "PRO is proposing to catch cheaters by destroying the surveillance network that catches cheaters." This took A's own A1 answer and turned it into a self-contradiction A never resolved.</best_rebuttal>
